Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- A former Colombian congressman who was held hostage in the jungle for more than eight years has escaped -- with the help of a former captor. Oscar Tulio Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. Oscar Tulio Lizcano, his hair disheveled, appeared too weak to stand for long when he met the news media Sunday, hours after stumbling onto a military patrol -- and freedom. Lizcano suffered from hunger and disease in captivity and endured isolation in the company of leftist rebels who often would not let him talk, he and Colombian authorities said. "Maybe my incoherence is for a lack of speaking," Lizcano told reporters. "I was unable to talk with the guerillas who guarded me." Lizcano said he had little to read in the jungle except "The Odyssey" by Homer. He suffered from malaria and other illnesses and once ate nothing but hearts of palm for six or seven days, said Juan Manuel Santos, the Colombian defense minister. "This is big news for the whole family," said Lizcano's sister, Amparo Lizcano. "We were waiting for the guerrillas to give our brother back alive before he died." The former congressman fled about three days ago with the assistance of one of his captors, a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, a leftist rebel force that has been fighting the government for more than 40 years in a war that also has involved right-wing paramilitaries and drug traffickers.  Watch release of FARC hostage » . President Alvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday with the ex-FARC rebel -- known by the alias "Isaza" -- and said the man will receive compensation and permission to resettle in France with his family. He said that's in keeping with a Colombian government policy that rewards rebels who desert and help hostages gain their freedom. Police officers and soldiers pinpointed the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months ago, Santos said. They monitored the location for about five months and took steps to seal off possible escape routes, he said, as they planned a rescue operation using information gleaned help from a rebel who deserted October 2. Troops started that rescue operation Saturday -- only to discover that "Isaza" and Lizcano had decided on their own to escape. The two men wandered through the jungle for three days and nights before encountering a Colombian army patrol Sunday, said Santos, the defense minister. Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. He and his former captor stumbled Sunday onto a patrol near the border of the states of Risaralda and Choco, in central Colombia, authorities said. The FARC holds an estimated 750 hostages in Colombia. Its members have justified hostage taking as a legitimate military tactic. The rebels have been battered this year by government raids that killed several top commanders, the death by apparent heart attack of their founder and a wave of desertions. Government commandoes tricked the FARC in July and freed their most prized hostage, the former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, in an elaborate ruse that also liberated three U.S. defense contractors and 11 other hostages. On Sunday, Lizcano offered words of encouragement to those hundreds who remain trapped in the jungle, captives of the FARC. "Hold on. Hold on," he said. "One day you will enjoy your freedom, too." -- CNN's Karl Penhaul contributed to this report .

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia (CNN) —** A former Colombian congressman who was held hostage in the jungle for more than eight years has escaped with the help of one of his former captors.

Oscar Tulio Lizcano, who was kidnapped near the Colombian town of Riosucio on August 4, 2000, appeared before the news media Sunday, just hours after he and his former captor stumbled upon a military patrol near the border between the central Colombian states of Risaralda and Chocó.

His hair disheveled, Lizcano appeared too weak to remain standing for long. He had suffered from hunger and disease while in captivity and endured isolation among leftist rebels who often forbade him from speaking, according to Lizcano and Colombian authorities.

“Maybe my incoherence is from a lack of speaking,” Lizcano told reporters. “I was unable to talk with the guerrillas who guarded me.”

Lizcano said he had little to read in the jungle apart from Homer’s *The Odyssey*. He suffered from malaria and other illnesses and, on one occasion, ate nothing but hearts of palm for six or seven days, Colombian Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos said.

“This is big news for the whole family,” said Lizcano’s sister, Amparo Lizcano. “We were waiting for the guerrillas to give our brother back alive before he died.”

The former congressman fled about three days earlier with the assistance of one of his captors, a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC. The leftist rebel group has fought the Colombian government for more than 40 years in a conflict that has also involved right-wing paramilitaries and drug traffickers.

*Watch the release of the FARC hostage »*

President Álvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday alongside the former FARC rebel, known by the alias “Isaza,” and said the man would receive compensation and permission to resettle in France with his family. Uribe said the arrangement was consistent with a Colombian government policy rewarding rebels who desert and help hostages gain their freedom.

Police officers and soldiers pinpointed the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months earlier, Santos said. They monitored the site for about five months and took steps to seal off possible escape routes while planning a rescue operation, using information obtained with the help of a rebel who deserted on October 2.

Troops launched the rescue operation Saturday, only to discover that Isaza and Lizcano had decided to escape on their own. The two men wandered through the jungle for three days and nights before encountering a Colombian army patrol Sunday, Santos said.

The FARC holds an estimated 750 hostages in Colombia. Its members have defended hostage-taking as a legitimate military tactic.

The rebel group has been battered this year by government raids that killed several senior commanders, the apparent heart-attack death of its founder, and a wave of desertions.

In July, government commandos deceived the FARC and freed its most prized hostage, former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, in an elaborate ruse that also secured the release of three U.S. defense contractors and 11 other hostages.

On Sunday, Lizcano offered words of encouragement to the hundreds who remain captive in the jungle.

“Hold on. Hold on,” he said. “One day you will enjoy your freedom, too.”

— CNN’s Karl Penhaul contributed to this report.

**BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) —** After spending more than eight years as a hostage in the Colombian jungle, former congressman Oscar Tulio Lizcano reached freedom with assistance from one of the rebels assigned to guard him.

Lizcano and his former captor encountered an army patrol Sunday near the border between the central Colombian states of Risaralda and Chocó. He had been abducted near Riosucio on August 4, 2000.

Appearing before reporters only hours after his escape, Lizcano had unkempt hair and seemed unable to remain standing for extended periods. He and Colombian officials said he had endured hunger, illness and severe isolation while being held by left-wing guerrillas, who frequently prevented him from speaking.

“My lack of coherence may be because I have not spoken,” he told journalists. “I could not converse with the guerrillas guarding me.”

According to Lizcano, Homer’s *The Odyssey* was virtually the only reading material available to him in the jungle. Colombian Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos said the former lawmaker contracted malaria and other diseases and, during one period lasting six or seven days, survived solely on hearts of palm.

For Lizcano’s relatives, his return brought enormous relief.

“This is wonderful news for the entire family,” said his sister, Amparo Lizcano. “We had been hoping the guerrillas would return our brother alive before he died.”

Lizcano escaped roughly three days before reaching the patrol. He was aided by a guard belonging to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known as the FARC. The leftist insurgent group has fought Colombia’s government for more than four decades in a conflict that has also included right-wing paramilitary organizations and drug traffickers.

*Watch the release of the FARC hostage.*

President Álvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday alongside the former FARC member, who uses the alias “Isaza.” Uribe announced that Isaza would be financially rewarded and allowed to relocate to France with his family. The president said the offer was consistent with a government program that compensates guerrillas who abandon the rebellion and assist captives in regaining their freedom.

Santos said police and military personnel had identified the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months earlier. Security forces watched the site for approximately five months and worked to block potential escape routes while preparing a rescue mission. Their planning relied in part on information provided by a rebel who deserted on October 2.

The operation began Saturday, but troops then learned that Lizcano and Isaza had already chosen to flee on their own. Santos said the pair spent three days and three nights making their way through the jungle before coming across the army patrol Sunday.

The FARC is believed to be holding about 750 people in Colombia, and the organization has defended kidnapping as a legitimate method of warfare.

During the year, however, the rebel group suffered significant setbacks. Government attacks killed several senior commanders, its founder apparently died of a heart attack, and many members deserted.

In July, Colombian commandos used an elaborate deception to fool the FARC and rescue its most prominent captive, former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt. The same mission also freed three American defense contractors and 11 additional hostages.

On Sunday, Lizcano addressed the hundreds of people who remain FARC prisoners in the jungle.

“Keep going. Keep going,” he said. “Someday, you too will experience freedom.”

— CNN’s Karl Penhaul contributed to this report.

FARC fighters kidnapped Lizcano in August 2000 from his home in Riosucio, in Colombia’s Caldas department. He became one of the longest-held political hostages in the rebel group’s decades-long conflict with the Colombian government.

Defense officials praised Bueno Largo for abandoning the FARC and said he would be eligible for benefits under a government program encouraging guerrillas to desert and provide assistance to authorities.

Lizcano’s escape came during a year of major setbacks for the FARC. Earlier in 2008, Colombian forces rescued former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American contractors and 11 Colombian security officers in an operation that infiltrated the rebels’ communications network.

The FARC had long used hostages as bargaining chips in an effort to secure the release of imprisoned guerrillas. Colombia’s government refused to create a demilitarized zone demanded by the rebels for negotiations.

# Colombian Hostage Óscar Tulio Lizcano Escapes FARC After Eight Years in Jungle

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia — October 26, 2008** — Former Colombian congressman Óscar Tulio Lizcano, weakened by years of illness, hunger and forced movement through the jungle, has escaped more than eight years of captivity with the help of one of his guards, a rebel deserter known by the alias **“Isaza,”** Colombian authorities announced Sunday.

Lizcano and the guerrilla, identified by officials as **Wilson Bueno Largo**, reached government forces in the western department of Chocó after trekking for several days through dense rainforest. Television images showed the former lawmaker gaunt, bearded and visibly exhausted but able to speak and embrace relatives and officials.

“I feel as if I have been reborn,” Lizcano told reporters after his rescue.

## Kidnapped from his home in 2000

Members of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or **FARC**, kidnapped Lizcano on August 5, 2000, from his home in the town of Riosucio, Caldas department. At the time, he was serving in Colombia’s House of Representatives.

The FARC regarded Lizcano as one of its politically valuable hostages and intended to use him in negotiations for the release of imprisoned guerrillas. For years, however, little reliable information emerged about his condition.

A proof-of-life video released during his captivity showed him looking extremely thin and suffering from poor health. His family repeatedly warned that he might die without medical attention.

## Disease, hunger and isolation

Lizcano said his health deteriorated badly in the jungle. He suffered bouts of **malaria and other tropical illnesses**, along with severe malnutrition and weakness. Reports from officials and relatives also indicated that he endured skin disease and gastrointestinal problems while receiving only rudimentary treatment.

Food was frequently scarce, he said, and the captives and their guards sometimes survived on whatever they could find. Constant military pressure forced the FARC unit to move repeatedly through rugged, rain-soaked terrain.

Lizcano described long periods of isolation in which he had little or no contact with other high-profile captives. At times, he said, his illness left him unsure whether he would survive.

“I was very sick,” he said. “There were moments when I thought I was going to die there.”

Colombian officials said he would undergo extensive medical examinations, with malnutrition and infectious disease among the immediate concerns.

## A guard turns against the FARC

The escape became possible when “Isaza,” one of the guerrillas assigned to guard Lizcano, decided to abandon the FARC and take the hostage with him.

According to initial accounts released by the government, the two slipped away from the rebel camp and spent roughly three days moving through the jungle while trying to avoid FARC patrols. They crossed difficult terrain with little food before encountering Colombian troops near **San José del Palmar in Chocó**.

Officials said the deserter carried a rifle and escorted Lizcano to safety rather than fleeing alone. The full circumstances of the escape were still being reviewed, and the men’s account could not immediately be independently verified.

Defense Minister **Juan Manuel Santos** praised the guerrilla’s decision, calling it evidence that government programs encouraging FARC fighters to desert were working.

## Government promises reward and protection

President **Álvaro Uribe’s** government welcomed Lizcano’s return as another major blow to the FARC, which had already lost several senior commanders and dozens of important hostages during 2008.

Authorities said Isaza would receive the benefits offered under Colombia’s demobilization program, including legal consideration and financial assistance. The government also said he could qualify for a substantial reward because he delivered a high-profile hostage alive.

Officials indicated that Isaza and his family would be given protection because of the risk of FARC retaliation. The government said it would also explore the possibility of arranging refuge abroad; France was discussed as a potential destination.

Uribe publicly urged other guerrillas guarding captives to follow Isaza’s example.

“Those who free hostages and abandon terrorism will be welcomed,” the president said, while warning that rebels who continued holding civilians would face sustained military pressure.

## Another setback for the FARC

Lizcano’s escape capped a disastrous year for Colombia’s largest guerrilla organization. In March, senior commander **Raúl Reyes** was killed in a Colombian military raid in Ecuador. FARC founder **Manuel Marulanda** died of natural causes, and another top commander, **Iván Ríos**, was killed by one of his own men.

In July, the Colombian military freed former presidential candidate **Íngrid Betancourt**, three American defense contractors and 11 Colombian soldiers and police officers in **Operation Jaque**, an intelligence operation in which soldiers posed as members of a humanitarian mission.

Lizcano’s return further strengthened the government’s argument that the FARC was fragmented, under pressure and increasingly vulnerable to desertions from within its own ranks.

The rebel group continued to hold members of the security forces and other captives, although the exact number remained disputed. Human-rights organizations have long condemned the FARC’s hostage-taking as a violation of international humanitarian law.

For Lizcano’s family, however, Sunday’s announcement ended more than eight years of uncertainty.

Standing before cameras after receiving medical attention, the former congressman thanked the soldier who helped him escape and the troops who found them.

His freedom, he said, came down to a decision by one guerrilla to stop guarding a prisoner and lead him home.

counterfactuals.output:
Óscar Tulio Lizcano, a former Colombian congressman, escaped from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) in October 2008 after being held for just over eight years. He had been kidnapped in August 2000 from his home region of Caldas.

His escape was made possible by one of his guards, Wilson Bueno Largo, known by the alias “Isaza,” who deserted the FARC and fled with him. They trekked for several days through dense jungle before encountering Colombian troops. Isaza later entered a government reintegration program and was offered a reward for helping free Lizcano.

Lizcano emerged severely weakened and emaciated. During captivity he had been moved repeatedly through remote jungle camps, often amid military pressure. He described chronic hunger, isolation, illness—including malaria—and punishing marches in rain and mud. At times he survived on very limited food and lost substantial weight.

The escape came during a period of major setbacks for the FARC. Earlier in 2008, Colombian forces had rescued Ingrid Betancourt, three U.S. contractors, and 11 members of the security forces in Operation Jaque. Senior FARC commanders had also been killed or had died, and desertions were increasing. The organization nevertheless still held hundreds of people, many for ransom, while a smaller group of politicians, soldiers, and police officers were regarded as “exchangeable” hostages whom the FARC hoped to trade for imprisoned guerrillas. Lizcano’s escape further highlighted both the harsh conditions endured by captives and the weakening control and morale within the guerrilla organization.
